intro: Read the deck for the arguments and these notes for the thinking. The notes under each slide explain it, give you something to remember and warn you where readers slip. At the end of each section, answer the questions without looking, test the ideas on a programme you know, and write your own notes in the space around mine.

sections.title: What ‘Decolonising Development’ Means
sections.big_idea: Decolonising development is an analysis of **who decides**, across knowledge, money, agenda, evaluation and representation. A new vocabulary changes nothing by itself.
in_plain_words: The word is everywhere, in funding calls and job descriptions, and used loosely it becomes a slogan. The course treats it as an analysis of how colonial power still shapes who develops whom, with whose knowledge and in whose interest. It works at three levels at once: knowledge, power and economy.

Five questions make it checkable against documents: whose theory counts, who sets the terms, who decided this was the problem, who defines success, and who tells the story. The sector's responses sit in three rows, cosmetic, reformist and radical. Apply one test throughout: **what changed in who decides?**

diagram.caption: five questions, each answerable from a document

key_terms.meaning: New words and images, same structures.
Real funding and hiring shifts inside the existing system.
Questions development itself.
The political struggle to end direct colonial rule.
Analysis of culture and identity after empire.
Coloniality outlived colonialism, so delink from its structures.

worked_example.title: Buzzword or analysis?
worked_example.setup: Four actions are proposed in one organisation. Apply the slide 4 test: after the change, who decides what counts as a problem, what counts as success, and where the money goes?
steps: A workshop on unconscious bias leaves all three untouched, so it is the buzzword use.
Diversifying a photo library changes presentation only, so it is also the buzzword use.
Moving a decision from London to Patna changes who decides, so it is an analysis in action.
Moving a budget line to a local partner changes where the money goes, so it passes too.
worked_example.answer: The first two change the presentation, and the last two change who decides.

mistakes: Treating new vocabulary as the change when the structure stays the same.
Reading decolonising as a rejection of all Western knowledge. The argument concerns hierarchy.
Romanticising the precolonial past. Those societies had their own hierarchies, caste among them.
Treating diversity and inclusion as the same thing. Those concern who is in the room, and decolonising concerns who decides.

recall.q: What are the three levels at which decolonising works?
recall.a: Knowledge, power and economy.

recall.q: Which three rows describe how the sector responds?
recall.a: Cosmetic, reformist and radical.

recall.q: Which tradition says colonialism ended while coloniality lives on?
recall.a: The decolonial school, with Quijano and Mignolo.

recall.q: Why can caste not be treated as a colonial import?
recall.a: It predates the British, though they reshaped it.

sections.title: The Colonial Roots of ‘Development’
sections.big_idea: ‘Development’ has **a history**. It descends from the civilising mission, and its categories and confidence carried over.
in_plain_words: Read the vocabulary from the nineteenth century to now: civilising, trusteeship, colonial welfare, technical assistance, partnership. The words soften while one party still assesses another's deficiency and offers to correct it. Continuity is not identity. Aid is not conquest, and the claim concerns the categories and the confidence.

Macaulay's 1835 Minute shows coloniality of knowledge in plain view. Truman's Point Four, announced on 20 January 1949, named most of the world underdeveloped. Escobar argues the category was invented as a norm, a measure, a label and a cure. After independence, **the colonial economy outlived the flag change** through trade, debt and land.

diagram.caption: how the relationship was named, century by century

key_terms.meaning: The claim that European rule uplifted backward peoples.
Truman's 1949 programme of aid for underdeveloped areas.
Macaulay's 1835 case for English-medium education.
A category that groups diverse societies by what they lack.
Terms attached to sovereign debt and aid.

worked_example.title: Spot what carried over
worked_example.setup: Three phrases from different eras appear in slide 13: ‘trusteeship over backward peoples’, ‘technical assistance to underdeveloped areas’ and ‘partnership’.
steps: For each phrase, ask who assesses whom.
In the first, one party judges another backward and takes charge.
In the second, one party judges another underdeveloped and offers technique.
In the third, the word is softer, yet the slide says one party still assesses another's deficiency and offers to correct it.
worked_example.answer: The vocabulary softens at each step while the structure persists.

mistakes: Claiming aid is colonial rule. The claim is that categories and confidence carried over.
Quoting Macaulay's line without his argument, which was a budget decision made on the stated ground that European knowledge was superior.
Overstating the invention. Hunger, disease and premature death were not invented in 1949.
Quoting the largest drain-of-wealth estimate without its method, which invites an easy dismissal.

recall.q: When did Truman announce Point Four?
recall.a: 20 January 1949, in his inaugural address.

recall.q: What did the third row of the Point Four table say it did?
recall.a: Offered technical knowledge as the remedy, so the problem became technical.

recall.q: Why did English education have mixed consequences?
recall.a: It produced the nationalist leadership and is a route out of caste hierarchy for many Dalit families.

recall.q: What overlapped almost exactly with the rise of development?
recall.a: The decolonisation of territory.

sections.title: Eurocentrism, Knowledge & Power
sections.big_idea: Knowledge and power **produce each other**. Defining a people is already a way of acting on them.
in_plain_words: Eurocentrism treats European history, categories and experience as the universal standard. Said showed how scholarship built the Orient as exotic, irrational and unchanging, a picture that flattered the West and justified rule. Escobar showed development working as a discourse that creates its own objects, such as the poor.

The categories carry the power. A threshold is set, people are counted against it, programmes are designed for the group, and success means crossing the line. Many supposedly universal ideas, such as the nuclear household and individual land title, are particular histories. Ask of every project **whose categories it works within**.

key_terms.meaning: Treating European categories as the universal standard.
Western scholarship's construction of ‘the Orient’.
A system of statements and institutions defining what can be thought.
A population recoded as a poverty line and indicators.
Asking where a ‘universal’ category came from and whom it fits.

worked_example.title: Read a proposal sentence
worked_example.setup: A draft says: ‘Deep-rooted cultural barriers keep beneficiaries from adopting best practice.’ Test it against the slide 24 table.
steps: ‘Deep-rooted cultural barriers’ casts the other as static and traditional.
‘Beneficiaries’ casts the other as passive, someone who receives.
‘Best practice’ casts the self as dynamic and rational.
Together they make outside intervention look necessary and local capacity invisible before any evidence is examined.
worked_example.answer: All three representational moves appear in one sentence.

mistakes: Reading the argument as a claim that evidence hierarchies are worthless. Trials answer certain questions well, and the claim concerns who decides which questions matter.
Taking Escobar to say people have no agency. A discourse shapes what is easy to say and leaves people free to resist.
Dropping every universal. Some, such as the rule that no one should be beaten, are worth defending.
Treating categories as avoidable. A food programme needs eligibility, and the identification creates a group.

recall.q: What did Said's Orientalism argue?
recall.a: Western scholarship constructed the Orient as exotic and static, justifying rule.

recall.q: What is a discourse?
recall.a: An organised system of statements, categories and institutions that defines what counts as true, normal and possible.

recall.q: Which fourth-row test shows a discourse at work?
recall.a: A funding application recommending no intervention does not fit the form.

recall.q: What does the slide 28 table do with the nuclear household?
recall.a: It shows it presented as universal while joint families and shared cooking are the lived arrangement.

sections.title: Critiques of the Mainstream
sections.big_idea: Three schools explain poverty differently, and all three **stay inside an economic frame** that leaves knowledge, race and being aside.
in_plain_words: Modernisation theory, associated with Rostow, pictures one ladder from traditional to high mass consumption and locates the obstacle inside poor societies. Dependency theory reverses the causation: poverty is produced by the same system that enriched the core. Wallerstein scales this to one world-system with a semi-periphery, which explains why countries change position.

Prebisch argued that terms of trade turn against exporters of primary goods, and Frank described one process that develops the metropole and underdevelops the satellite. The policy record is mixed. Even these critics kept industrial growth as the aim and the nation-state as the unit, so **caste, gender and region stayed invisible**.

key_terms.meaning: Development as one linear path that poor countries follow.
Peripheral economies shaped by the needs of core economies.
The price of exports relative to imports.
A zone that both exploits and is exploited.
Detaching from the world system, as Amin proposed.

worked_example.title: Which school says it?
worked_example.setup: Match three statements from the slide 33 and 35 tables to a school.
steps: ‘Poverty is a starting condition and integration helps’ belongs to modernisation.
‘Integration on unequal terms is the mechanism’ belongs to dependency.
‘A state that is victim and extractor at once’ describes the semi-periphery in world-systems analysis.
What the three share: an economic frame that takes industrial growth as the aim.
worked_example.answer: Modernisation, dependency, world-systems, and a shared economic frame.

mistakes: Reading ‘behind’ as a neutral description. The slide says that it turns a political relationship into a chronological one.
Treating dependency policy as a success. Import substitution produced protected, inefficient industries in several countries.
Assuming the critics questioned the aim. Dependency inverted the explanation and left industrial growth intact.
Applying a nation-level theory to caste, gender or region inside the nation.

recall.q: What did Rostow's stages hold?
recall.a: All societies climb from traditional to high mass consumption if they adopt Western institutions.

recall.q: What did Prebisch argue?
recall.a: Terms of trade move against commodity exporters over time.

recall.q: Where does the deck place India and China in Wallerstein's scheme?
recall.a: Largely in the semi-periphery.

recall.q: What do the decolonial thinkers add?
recall.a: Knowledge, race and being.

sections.title: Coloniality
sections.big_idea: Colonialism was **a political event** that ended. Coloniality is the pattern of power it left, and it continues.
in_plain_words: The decolonial school separates two things usually merged. Colonialism is rule by a foreign power, with a date. Coloniality is reproduced by institutions, categories and elites after independence, including domestic elites, which is why independence did not dissolve it.

Quijano traced a structure born with conquest that organises labour, knowledge, authority and being around a racial hierarchy. It has three faces: power, knowledge and being. Mignolo adds that there is no modernity without coloniality, and offers delinking and border thinking as an option among others. The framework was built around race in Latin America, so **it must be re-fitted to caste** here.

right.title: Coloniality
items: A pattern of power that outlived it

key_terms.meaning: Labour and authority sorted by a racial hierarchy.
Whose ways of knowing count as science.
Whose humanity is taken for granted.
Detaching from the assumption that European categories are the only valid ones.
Thinking from the position the frame excludes.

worked_example.title: Which face is it?
worked_example.setup: Sort four observations using the slide 42 table.
steps: Caste and the division of labour: coloniality of power.
English-medium expertise: coloniality of knowledge.
Whose deaths are counted, and how: coloniality of being.
Direct rule by an occupying power: that is colonialism itself, and it has an end date.
worked_example.answer: Power, knowledge and being are the faces of coloniality, and occupation is colonialism.

mistakes: Saying coloniality is caused only by external actors. Domestic elites and institutions reproduce it.
Trying to decolonise the economy and leaving knowledge and being untouched.
Importing a framework built around race into South Asia without re-fitting it to caste.
Treating Mignolo's option as a universal programme. He declines to offer one.

recall.q: What did Maldonado-Torres write about coloniality?
recall.a: Coloniality survives colonialism.

recall.q: What is the hubris of the zero point?
recall.a: Pretending to a view from nowhere that is actually a view from the centre of power.

recall.q: Name one measured fact about who produces knowledge.
recall.a: Studies find research about a country is often written without authors from it.

recall.q: What is the standard objection to Mignolo?
recall.a: A position defined by refusal is hard to turn into a programme.

sections.title: Whose Knowledge Counts
sections.big_idea: Knowledge has a hierarchy that is rarely stated and constantly enacted. **Assess reliability** and do not assign it by position.
in_plain_words: A randomised trial counts as evidence while a farmer's account of the same intervention is filed as opinion. Fricker names the harm: testimonial injustice discounts a speaker because of who they are, and hermeneutical injustice leaves a group without words for its experience. The second is invisible, so a form with fixed categories records only anticipated harms.

Spivak asks whether the subaltern can be heard within structures built by power. The practical residue is a methods note: say who selected speakers, who translated and who edited. Local knowledge is tested knowledge produced outside the academy, though some practice is harmful and **assessment beats assumption** in both directions. Ngũgĩ extends the argument to language.

diagram.caption: from being doubted to authoring the work

key_terms.meaning: Harm done to someone specifically as a knower.
A speaker given less credibility because of who they are.
No shared concept exists to name an experience.
The most marginalised, within structures of colonial and patriarchal power.
Representing others in the expert's terms.

worked_example.title: Speaking for or making space?
worked_example.setup: Classify four actions with the slide 51 table.
steps: You summarise their view in a meeting: speaking for.
They meet the donor directly: making space.
You write the case study: speaking for.
They are the author, are paid and approve what is published: making space.
worked_example.answer: Two of the four actions speak for people, and two make space.

mistakes: Reading Spivak as saying the subaltern cannot talk. She argues that the structures of hearing are missing.
Treating local knowledge as automatically correct. The slide calls that its own kind of condescension.
Speaking for people by default and never asking whether the other column was possible.
Consulting a community and publishing what you learn without agreement, which is extraction.

recall.q: What is the difference between testimonial and hermeneutical injustice?
recall.a: One discounts the speaker, and the other leaves no concept to name the harm.

recall.q: Why is the right-hand column of speaking for versus making space rare?
recall.a: It costs money and time: travel, translation and fees.

recall.q: What did Ngũgĩ do with his creative work?
recall.a: Renounced English for Gikuyu.

recall.q: What decolonial test does the language slide give?
recall.a: In whose language is the agenda set, and who needs a translator to question the plan?

sections.title: Decolonising Aid & the NGO Sector
sections.big_idea: Whoever holds the purse holds the power. **Money, accountability and prestige rise** while risk and delivery sink.
in_plain_words: Aid runs from donors to international NGOs to national NGOs to communities. Priorities flow down and reports flow up, grant cycles are short, and overheads are capped, which lets local partners deliver projects and keeps them from becoming durable institutions. Risk moves to the smallest party.

Teju Cole's white-saviour industrial complex describes a structure in which the rescuer's image takes the centre, and the same dynamic runs between metropolitan professionals and rural communities. Localisation and #ShiftThePower aim to move funding and decisions. The 2016 Grand Bargain target of 25% is **persistently missed**, and ‘as directly as possible’ lets intermediaries report progress without moving decision rights.

diagram.caption: the aid chain: money up, risk down

key_terms.meaning: Shifting funding, decisions and leadership to local actors.
The 2016 humanitarian pledge, with a 25% direct-funding target.
A movement for community control of resources.
‘We know what they need’.
Reporting first to the communities served.

worked_example.title: How far is the Grand Bargain target?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 400 units of humanitarian funding pass through the system, and the target is 25% as directly as possible to local responders. Suppose 16 units reach local actors directly.
steps: Target: 400 × 0.25 = 100 units.
Reached directly: 16 ÷ 400 = 0.04, which is 4%.
Gap: 100 − 16 = 84 units.
The slide says the real share has stayed in low single digits, and funds routed through intermediaries can be reported while decision rights stay put.
worked_example.answer: 4% against a 25% target, a gap of 84 units on these illustrative figures.

mistakes: Treating the localisation percentage as a measure of power. The percentage and the decision rights do not track each other.
Assuming people cannot be trusted with cash. Studies find recipients spend on food, health, education and assets.
Treating white saviourism as a matter of individual sincerity when the incentives produce it.
Describing a capped overhead as pure efficiency when it blocks institution building.

recall.q: Name two rows of the aid chain table.
recall.a: Any two of: donor priorities, short grant cycles, upward reporting, capped overheads, downward risk.

recall.q: What is the Grand Bargain target?
recall.a: 25% of humanitarian funding as directly as possible to local responders.

recall.q: What does #ShiftThePower add to localisation?
recall.a: Community control of resources, with untied core funding and Southern-led agendas.

recall.q: Why is the honest tension hard to escape?
recall.a: Organisations are asked to give away the funds and visibility that sustain them.

sections.title: Decolonising Research & Data
sections.big_idea: Research is rarely neutral. The test is whether it was done **with a community or on one**.
in_plain_words: Who funds the study, frames the question, holds the data and signs the paper are all expressions of power. Tuhiwai Smith calls research one of the dirtiest words in the indigenous world's vocabulary. Helicopter research arrives, collects and leaves, which mirrors the colonial commodity economy in data form.

Each alternative is a budget line and a contract clause: a local partner from design, named local co-authors, shared custody, findings returned in the local language. Data sovereignty says communities may govern data about them, and the CARE principles complement FAIR by asking who holds authority. **Ask who counts as the community** before consent is taken.

diagram.caption: they sit beside FAIR and add the question of authority

key_terms.meaning: Drop in, gather data and leave, publishing elsewhere.
The right of peoples to govern data about them.
Collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, ethics.
Findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable.
Participants shape the question and act on findings.

worked_example.title: Apply CARE to an open dataset
worked_example.setup: A team plans to publish a village survey openly. Check it with the four CARE letters.
steps: Collective benefit: does the dataset benefit the people it describes?
Authority to control: did the community agree to indefinite reuse by anyone?
Responsibility: are those working with the data accountable to the community?
Ethics: do rights and wellbeing come before openness? FAIR alone answers only the technical question.
worked_example.answer: Openness is progress against one hierarchy and can be extraction under another.

mistakes: Treating the village as one authority. A dominant-caste panchayat consenting for Dalit households reproduces the problem.
Budgeting nothing for returning findings, the clearest marker of research done on a community.
Negotiating authorship after the results exist, when it becomes a favour from whoever holds the draft.
Calling a participatory process community voice when the same men who dominate other forums attend.

recall.q: What is the fourth row irony in the research decisions table?
recall.a: Research done in a country is often published where its institutions cannot afford to read it.

recall.q: What do the four CARE letters stand for?
recall.a: Collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility and ethics.

recall.q: What is the six-month test for findings?
recall.a: Does the community have anything from the study, or only a memory of being surveyed?

recall.q: Which grant mechanism works best for change?
recall.a: Funder conditions, since what a grant condition requires happens.

sections.title: Post-Development & Alternatives
sections.big_idea: Post-development questions **the goal as well as the method**, but the alternatives agree more on what they reject than on what to build.
in_plain_words: Escobar, Sachs, Esteva and Rahnema argue the whole project should be abandoned. The strongest objection is that child mortality, literacy and life expectancy have improved across South Asia. The serious version of the argument accepts material improvement and rejects one model of the good life, one measure and one set of experts.

The alternatives come from different places: buen vivir from the Andes, ubuntu from Southern Africa, swaraj and swadeshi from Gandhi, degrowth from a Northern critique, and the pluriverse from the Zapatistas. Ambedkar's objection to village self-sufficiency is the warning: **an indigenous alternative can carry an indigenous hierarchy**.

diagram.root: Alternatives to growth as the goal

children.label: Buen vivir
items: Living well, in balance with nature

diagram.caption: plus the pluriverse: many worlds fit

key_terms.meaning: A world where many worlds fit.
Good living together, in balance with community and nature.
A person is a person through other persons.
Self-rule, down to the village.
Rich economies reduce material throughput.

worked_example.title: Pair each claim with its objection
worked_example.setup: Use the slide 75 table to match three post-development claims with the objection raised.
steps: ‘Development is a project to be abandoned’ meets the objection that people want clinics, schools and electricity.
‘Its promise has failed on its own terms’ meets the objection that poverty and mortality have fallen substantially.
‘Alternatives already exist locally’ meets the objection that some are hierarchical in their own right.
The slide calls the second objection the strongest.
worked_example.answer: Each claim has a named objection, and the second is the strongest.

mistakes: Hearing degrowth as a proposal that poor countries stay poor. Its serious proponents aim contraction at high-consuming economies.
Treating a constitutional principle as an achieved alternative. Ecuador and Bolivia expanded extraction after enshrining buen vivir.
Romanticising the village. Ambedkar called it a sink of localism, and for Dalits it was a site of oppression.
Reading the pluriverse as a programme when the deck calls the absence of a single alternative the point.

recall.q: When did Ecuador and Bolivia write buen vivir into their constitutions?
recall.a: Ecuador in 2008 and Bolivia in 2009.

recall.q: What did Gandhi's Hind Swaraj reject?
recall.a: The Western industrial model itself.

recall.q: What do the five alternatives share?
recall.a: A refusal of the single, growth-defined, Western destination.

recall.q: Where is degrowth's argument aimed?
recall.a: At rich economies, which are to contract.

sections.title: Decolonising Practice
sections.big_idea: Decolonising is finally a set of small choices that **move power**: how programmes are funded, designed, staffed, spoken and judged.
in_plain_words: The changes run from easy to hard. Anyone can stop writing ‘beneficiary’ today. A project manager can send findings back in the local language. A director can change who signs off the indicators, and moving a budget line takes a board and a funder. The risk is stopping at the easy ones.

Test partnership by asking who can say no in the next big decision. Overheads capped below real cost state your position in a number. Unrestricted multi-year grants, full cost recovery and direct funding move decisions with the money. Run the self-audit, since **every question has a documentary answer**.

diagram.caption: four shifts, ordered by the authority they need

key_terms.meaning: Funding a partner's real costs, including core costs.
Decisions made by those affected.
Reporting to communities as well as funders.
Dignity-stripping imagery used for donations.
Seven questions answered from documents.

worked_example.title: Who can make the change?
worked_example.setup: Order five changes from slide 84 by the authority each needs.
steps: Stop writing ‘beneficiary’: anyone, today.
Put a local co-author on the next report: a researcher or programme lead.
Send findings back in the local language: a project manager with a small budget line.
Change who signs off the indicators: a director.
Move a budget line to a local partner: a board, and a funder.
worked_example.answer: The first three need no one's permission, and the last two need senior authority.

mistakes: Stopping at language changes. A glossary with no other change is a style guide.
Capping a partner's indirect costs at a rate you would not accept for yourself.
Anonymising people by default. It can erase the person who wanted their name on the story.
Answering the self-audit with values statements when the questions have documents behind them.

recall.q: What is the test of real partnership on slide 86?
recall.a: In the next big decision, who can actually say no?

recall.q: What does unrestricted funding allow?
recall.a: An organisation to pursue what it judges important, which separates an institution from a contractor.

recall.q: What consent standard does the representation table give?
recall.a: Informed, specific, revocable and revisited for reuse.

recall.q: Which document answers who set the indicators?
recall.a: The results framework.

sections.title: Tensions, Critiques & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: A good course **turns the critique on itself**. Decolonial thought is powerful and incomplete, so hold it beside class, caste and gender.
in_plain_words: The serious objections are listed with weights: strong on diagnosis and thin on programme, attributing to colonialism what predates it, produced in Northern universities, able to excuse domestic elites, and hard to read for the people it concerns. The fourth has most force in South Asia. Romanticising ‘the local’ ignores caste and patriarchy, and essentialising ‘the West’ and ‘the indigenous’ rebuilds the binary of Orientalism.

Co-optation is the sharpest danger: the language is adopted and the structures stay. Judge by power and money moved. The hardest question, whether a colonial sector can decolonise itself, has a pessimist, a pragmatist and a third view that the sector is the wrong unit. The deck does not resolve it, and **Ambedkar belongs in the canon**.

left.title: The pessimist
items: The aid system is the colonial relation

right.title: The pragmatist
items: Those inside can shift power now

key_terms.meaning: Treating local structures as harmonious and just.
Treating West and indigenous as fixed, pure, opposed essences.
Bhabha's point that traditions are mixed and entangled.
Adopting the language and leaving the structures.
Refusing to accept whose knowledge counts.

worked_example.title: Reality-check a claim
worked_example.setup: A speaker says ‘the community knows best’. Use the slide 93 table.
steps: Ask which community, and who speaks for it.
Recall that the community is not a harmonious whole.
For a Dalit household the distant state has sometimes been a protection against local domination.
Devolving authority to the village can then transfer it to people already dominant there.
worked_example.answer: The claim needs the question ‘which community?’ before it can guide action.

mistakes: Locating all responsibility in the colonial past, which is comfortable for domestic elites.
Using ‘Western imposition’ to resist women's rights or caste reform and calling it decolonial.
Asking one person from a region to speak for it.
Assigning decolonisation work to staff of colour on top of their jobs and without resources.

recall.q: Which objection has most force in South Asia?
recall.a: That the analysis can excuse present-day domestic elites.

recall.q: What does Lorde's warning say?
recall.a: The master's tools will never dismantle the master's house.

recall.q: How should co-optation be detected?
recall.a: By power and money moved, never by the vocabulary used.

recall.q: Which five points does the final slide list?
recall.a: Colonial roots, coloniality outliving colonialism, knowledge as power, following money and decisions, and naming internal hierarchies.

notes.2: The course has two halves. Sections 02 to 06 diagnose, and sections 07 to 10 respond. Section 11 turns the critique on itself. Read the diagnosis first, because **the practical sections answer the problems it names**.
notes.4: Test every use of the word by the right-hand column. After the change, who decides what counts as a problem, what counts as success, and where the money goes? **A change of presentation** leaves those three untouched. Keep this test for the whole course.
notes.5: Memorise the five questions: knowledge, money, agenda, evaluation, representation. Each has an answer you can check in a document, so it cannot dissolve into a mood. Apply them to your own organisation first. The **agenda** row determines everything downstream.
notes.6: Use the two tables to separate what decolonising is from the confusions around it. The first table describes structure, discomfort and a shift of power. The second lists common conflations, and the fourth, diversity and inclusion, is **the most common in practice**.
notes.7: Keep the three traditions apart. Anti-colonial movements ended colonial rule, postcolonial writers analyse culture after empire, and decolonial thinkers argue that **coloniality outlived colonialism**. The deck leans on the third because it explains why independent states reproduce old hierarchies.
notes.8: South Asia holds both the experience of empire and the thinking against it. The table lists inheritances still visible today. Look hardest at the **census categories**, and remember that caste predates the British, so treating every hierarchy as colonial is wrong.
notes.9: Sort responses into three rows. Cosmetic changes language and photographs, reformist shifts real funding and hiring inside the system, and radical questions development itself. Place your own organisation on the table. **Most available movement** is from row one to row two.
notes.10: Four questions precede any project: who defines the problem, who sets the goal, whose knowledge counts, who owns the resources. The right-hand column shows questions no programme can answer. **The sector funds what it can answer**, and that decides which problems count as real.
notes.11: Use the roadmap for the shape of the course: diagnosis first, then response. Within the response sit aid, research, alternatives and practice. Keep the diagnosis in mind later, because **each practical shift answers a problem named earlier**.
notes.13: Read the right-hand column from top to bottom. The vocabulary softens at each step while one party still assesses another's deficiency and offers to correct it. That **continuity** is a claim you can check historically. Remember the caution that aid is not conquest.
notes.14: Strip the racial language from the civilising mission and a structure remains: an advanced party guiding a deficient one toward a **single, predefined destination**. The slide says that structure migrated into development. Use it as a test whenever a programme assumes one path for everyone.
notes.15: Macaulay's Minute is a budget argument for funding one kind of education, made on the stated ground that European knowledge was superior. Read it in full, since the reasoning is open. The consequences were mixed: the same education **produced the nationalist leaders** and offers many Dalit families a route out of caste hierarchy.
notes.16: On 20 January 1949, Truman's Point Four named most of the world underdeveloped. Row three has the longest shadow: poverty became **a shortfall of technique**, so experts and projects could fix it and trade, debt and land left the conversation. Remember the Cold War context in row four.
notes.17: Escobar's point is that underdevelopment was invented as a category through four steps: a norm, a measure, a label and a cure. The fourth step **self-perpetuates**, because institutions form around the category. He accepts that hunger and disease are real. What was invented was a way of grouping and explaining them.
notes.18: Plans, experts and aid institutions multiplied after 1949, from the Bretton Woods bodies to five-year plans. Notice the timing: **decolonisation of territory and the rise of development overlapped almost exactly**. As flags changed, subtler external guidance arrived.
notes.19: Compare the two columns: inherited structures and new dependencies. Independence moved political authority and left railways, crop mix and land relations in place for generations. Treat the drain of wealth with care, since estimates vary by method, and **quote a figure only with its basis**.
notes.20: Four lines to memorise. Development is recent, born around 1949. It inherited the hierarchy of the civilising mission. Underdevelopment was constructed and then treated as fact. Decolonising means **seeing this history inside today's practice**.
notes.22: Knowledge and power produce each other, so describing a people is already a way of acting on them. Study the four decisions: evidence, language, certification, theory. The fourth is sharpest, since **the same intellectual act is filed as general theory or as regional knowledge**.
notes.23: Said argued in 1978 that Western scholarship built the Orient as exotic, irrational and unchanging, a mirror that flattered the West and justified ruling over it. Remember his line that **the Orient was almost a European invention**. The next slide shows how the loop works.
notes.24: Follow the four-step loop: the West writes about the East, defines it as inferior, uses the definition to justify rule, and rule yields more knowledge. Then read your own last proposal against the right-hand column. **Most practitioners find at least two of those phrases.**
notes.25: Escobar treated development as a discourse, a system of knowledge, institutions and practices that produces its own objects, such as the poor and the Third World. His quoted line says it created a space where only certain things could be said. **Read the quotation twice** before the next slide.
notes.26: A discourse decides what counts as true, normal and possible. Try the test in the fourth row: write a funding application recommending that no intervention is warranted, and notice the form cannot hold it. A discourse **constrains what is easy to say**, and people still resist.
notes.27: Walk the five steps: a line is set, people are counted, the category acquires characteristics, programmes are designed for it, and success means crossing the line. The line can be moved. Categories are necessary, so ask **who drew them and what they hide**.
notes.28: Ask of each left-hand item where it came from and whom it fits. The nuclear household, individual land title, wage work and written contracts are particular histories presented as universal. Then keep the counter-argument: some universals, such as **no one should be beaten**, are worth defending.
notes.29: Hold two questions together: does this project work, and whose categories is it working within? Said shows that representation can be a form of rule, and Escobar shows that development makes its own objects. **The frame is open to inquiry as well as the project.**
notes.31: Rostow's stages picture one ladder for every society. Look at row two, where the politics sits: if the obstacle is internal, trade terms, debt and capital flows drop out of the explanation. The logic survives in any theory of change that **locates every constraint inside the community**.
notes.32: Four hidden assumptions: one direction, tradition as obstacle, poor countries as early, the West as the future. The deepest move puts the cause of poverty inside poor societies. Chakrabarty's phrase, the **waiting room of history**, names what the timeline does with a political question.
notes.33: Dependency theory reverses the causation: poverty is produced by the same global system that enriched the core. Modernisation and dependency both want poverty to end. They differ on causes, and **different causes produce different policy**, such as more aid versus changed terms.
notes.34: Prebisch argued that terms of trade turn against commodity exporters, so trading more of the same makes you poorer. Frank saw one process developing the metropole and underdeveloping the satellite. The record is mixed: **import substitution** often protected inefficient industries.
notes.35: Wallerstein's semi-periphery explains movement, which a rigid two-zone model cannot. Learn the three zones by role: the core captures value, the semi-periphery both exploits and is exploited, the periphery supplies raw materials. The slide places **India and China largely in the semi-periphery**.
notes.36: Read across the three columns. Modernisation takes the nation alone and locates the cause inside. Dependency and world-systems take the whole system and locate it outside. The closing line matters: poverty becomes **a relation**, which prepares the idea of coloniality.
notes.37: The critics changed the explanation and left the aim alone. Dependency theorists still wanted industrial growth, still took the nation-state as the unit and still relied on expert planning. A **nation-level theory cannot see caste, gender or region** inside the nation.
notes.38: Three lenses on one gap, all economic. Modernisation says catch up, dependency says extraction, and world-systems says one system with a core and a periphery. The last line is your bridge: **the decolonial turn adds knowledge, race and being**.
notes.40: Learn the separation: colonialism was a political event with an end date, and coloniality is the pattern of power it left behind. The fourth row is uncomfortable, since coloniality is reproduced by **domestic elites and institutions** as well as outsiders. That is why independence did not dissolve it.
notes.41: Quijano defines coloniality of power as the structure born with conquest that organises labour, knowledge, authority and being around a racial hierarchy. His claim is that the modern idea of race was invented to **naturalise colonial domination**, and the order it created still sorts the world.
notes.42: Power, knowledge and being are three faces of one structure, so you cannot decolonise the economy and leave the other two alone. The third face asks whose suffering registers. Remember the warning that a framework built around race in Latin America must be **re-fitted to caste**.
notes.43: Mignolo says there is no modernity without coloniality. His terms are delinking, border thinking and epistemic disobedience, offered as one option among others. Notice the standard objection: a position built on refusal is **stronger at diagnosis than at what to do on Monday**.
notes.44: A single image to memorise: modernity and coloniality are two sides of one coin. Progress, reason and markets sit on the bright face, and conquest, race and extraction on the dark one. **The bright face requires the dark.**
notes.45: Knowledge is presented as placeless yet produced from somewhere, mostly a handful of Northern institutions. The fourth row is measurable, since Southern scholars often appear as data collectors. The remedies start with **authorship agreements before fieldwork**.
notes.46: Coloniality outlives colonialism: the structure persists after the flag has gone. Quijano names the racial hierarchy that organises power, knowledge and being, and Mignolo says to delink and think from the border. The task is therefore **a different relation to power and knowledge**.
notes.48: The left column holds an RCT, a consultant's report, published seed data and a donor's theory of change. The right holds the farmer's account, the field worker's observation, generations of seed selection and the community's history. **Assess reliability instead of assigning it by position.**
notes.49: Keep Fricker's two forms apart. Testimonial injustice discounts a speaker because of who they are. Hermeneutical injustice means no shared concept exists to name the harm. The second is **invisible**, so a form with fixed categories records only anticipated harms. An open field and a listener let others in.
notes.50: Spivak's essay is quoted more than read, and the table corrects three misreadings. Her target is intellectuals who claim to convey the voices of the oppressed transparently. The practical residue is a **methods note**: say who selected the speakers, who translated, who edited and what was left out.
notes.51: Compare speaking for with making space row by row. The right-hand column costs travel, translation and fees, which is the honest reason it is rare. Speaking for is sometimes right, where attendance is unsafe or someone asked you to. The failure is **doing it by default**.
notes.52: Local knowledge in agro-ecology, medicine, ecology and governance is tested knowledge produced outside the academy. The last row is the honest one: some practice is effective and some harmful, so the call is for **assessment without assumption**. Documenting and patenting it without agreement is extraction.
notes.53: Ngũgĩ argues that the deepest colonial weapon was control of culture and language. He renounced English for Gikuyu in his own creative work. Keep his sentence in mind: the bullet was the means of physical subjugation and **language the means of spiritual subjugation**.
notes.54: The test is in whose language the agenda is set. Row three shapes the sector: English grant-writing is a specialised skill, so money follows it and calls the result merit. Hold the complication on this slide: for many Dalit families **English has been a way around a vernacular hierarchy**.
notes.55: Four lines to hold. Some people are doubted simply as knowers. Beware speaking for others, and dismantle what silences them. Indigenous and local knowledge are knowledge. Ngũgĩ asks us to decolonise the mind and **the language of the work**.
notes.57: Follow the chain from donor to INGO to local NGO to community. Money, accountability and prestige rise to the top while risk sinks to the bottom. The fourth row is the quiet one: **capped overheads** let local partners deliver projects and keep them from becoming durable institutions.
notes.58: Teju Cole's phrase describes a pattern in which the rescuer's feelings and image take the centre. The poster child has no name and the volunteer is the protagonist. It describes a structure, so it appears among well-meaning people. The same dynamic runs between **metropolitan Indian professionals and rural communities**.
notes.59: Paternalism sounds like ‘they need to be sensitised first’. The first row is the best-tested claim, and studies of unconditional cash transfers find recipients spend on food, health, education and assets, with **no systematic rise in alcohol or tobacco**. Use the slide's test: would we say it about people like us?
notes.60: The chart is illustrative and shows where decision power sits along the chain. The pattern is the point: those closest to the problem hold the least say. Treat it as **a picture of the argument**. The slide labels it illustrative, so quote no figure from it.
notes.61: The Grand Bargain of 2016 set a target of 25% of funding as directly as possible to local responders. The directly funded share has stayed in low single digits by most counts. **As directly as possible** is the clause doing the work, because intermediaries can report against the target while decision rights stay put.
notes.62: #ShiftThePower goes beyond localisation to community philanthropy, untied core funding and Southern-led agendas. Row three repays thought: an organisation funded by local giving has **a constituency that can withdraw**. The slide also names the limit, which is that it shifts power and leaves distribution unsolved.
notes.63: The tension is plain: organisations are asked to give away the funds and visibility that sustain them. Row two is a real constraint, since charity law places legal duties on control and reporting. Row four is hardest, reform led by those with most to lose. That is why **incentives and donor rules** matter.
notes.64: Four lines. The aid chain concentrates power at the top. White saviourism centres the rescuer. Localisation pledges outrun the money that follows. #ShiftThePower asks you to untie funding, flip accountability and **cede the agenda**.
notes.66: Funding, framing, data and authorship are all expressions of power. Tuhiwai Smith calls research one of the dirtiest words in the indigenous world's vocabulary. The last row is the most fixable: **returning findings** costs a visit and a translation, and it marks whether research was done with a community.
notes.67: Helicopter research drops in, collects and leaves, publishing elsewhere. The slide compares it with the colonial commodity economy in data form. Every alternative is a budget line and a contract clause, so you can **check it in documents**. Grant conditions work where ethics statements do not.
notes.68: This chart is illustrative and shows a directional pattern: Northern institutions are over-represented as lead and senior authors of research about the South. Studies of global-health and development literature report it repeatedly. Use it to ask **who wrote the paper you are citing**.
notes.69: Data sovereignty says peoples have the right to govern data about them. Walk the four questions, from who holds the raw data to who may withdraw it, and compare usual with better answers. Open data adds a complication: **openness answers the technical question and leaves authority open**.
notes.70: Learn CARE as four words: collective benefit, authority to control, responsibility, ethics. It complements the FAIR principles by asking who has authority over data about a people. Watch the last paragraph: **a dominant-caste panchayat** consenting for Dalit households reproduces the problem inside the remedy.
notes.71: Compare the two modes. The extractive default sends results away behind a paywall, and decolonial practice returns findings in usable form and local language with co-authorship. Apply the six-month test: does the community hold anything from the study? The costs are **a day, an afternoon, a conversation**.
notes.72: Participatory approaches shift who shapes the question. They are slower and not automatically better, because whoever already holds authority can capture the process. **Ask who participated.** If the same men who dominate other forums take part, the method has recorded the existing hierarchy as community voice.
notes.73: Research with a community differs from research on one. Remember the five lines: research carries power, helicopter studies extract, data sovereignty and CARE matter, findings go back, and **the community is a partner** in the work.
notes.75: Post-development thinkers argue the whole project should be abandoned. Read the objections beside each claim. The strongest is the second: child mortality, literacy and life expectancy have improved across South Asia. The serious version is narrower: **welcome the material gains** while questioning one model, one measure and one set of experts.
notes.76: The pluriverse comes from the Zapatistas: a world where many worlds fit. It stands against the one-world, one-future model of development. Remember its promise as the **dignity of many paths in place of one better path**.
notes.77: Buen vivir means living well together, in balance with community and nature. It is in the constitutions of Ecuador (2008) and Bolivia (2009). The test is row four: both states later expanded extractive industry. Read that as evidence about implementation, since a principle without **a fiscal alternative** loses to revenue.
notes.78: Ubuntu holds that a person is a person through other persons. It makes wellbeing relational, so my flourishing is tied to yours. Use it as a **direct challenge to the individualism** at development's core, and compare it with the other alternatives on slide 81.
notes.79: Gandhi's swaraj and swadeshi rejected the Western industrial model itself. Pair them with Ambedkar's objection that the village was a site of oppression for Dalits. The slide's lesson is the danger in section 11: **an indigenous alternative can carry an indigenous hierarchy**.
notes.80: Degrowth is a Northern critique that rich economies should shrink their material throughput. It is often misheard as a proposal that poor countries stay poor, and serious proponents say the opposite. The South Asian question is **who reduces first**, since environmental limits have been used to constrain the South.
notes.81: Five alternatives, one refusal. They agree on what they reject: GDP as the measure, a single path, nature as mere resource and expertise located outside. They differ on the state, markets, tradition and scale. The honest summary is that **they agree on rejection more than on replacement**.
notes.82: Post-development questions the goal along with the method. Buen vivir, ubuntu and swaraj are locally rooted visions of a good life. Degrowth challenges growth as a goal, starting in the North. **The pluriverse is a world where many worlds fit.**
notes.84: Read the table by the authority each change needs. You can stop writing ‘beneficiary’ today, and moving a budget line takes a board and a funder. The closing warning matters: language and co-authorship are real and small. An organisation that stops there sits in **row one** of the spectrum.
notes.85: Changing words forces the underlying relation into view. Use the table for the swaps: participant for beneficiary, the specific skill for capacity building, the place by name for the field. The failure mode is **a glossary and no other change**, which produces a style guide.
notes.86: Test partnership with one question: in the next big decision, who can say no? Then check the table row by row. Overheads are the concrete test, since a cap on a partner's indirect costs states your position in a number. Write into agreements **who bears an audit finding**.
notes.87: Funding is where decolonising becomes a fight over grant agreements. Unrestricted multi-year grants signal trust and let a partner become an institution. Each row costs a funder control or comparability. Unrestricted funding marks the difference between **an institution and a contractor**.
notes.88: Whoever sets the indicators has already decided what the programme is for. Shift the four questions toward participants: who defines success, what counts as evidence, who evaluates, who reads the report. Try the cheap test: write down what would make it **worth participants' time** and report against it.
notes.89: Treat representation as a decolonial question. The standards table covers consent, naming, payment, approval and framing. The second row runs against instinct, since anonymising by default can erase a person. Images of helplessness raise more money, so the **incentive runs against the standard**.
notes.90: This is a usable audit because every question has a documentary answer: the proposal, the results framework, the agreement, the org chart, minutes, the distribution list, the data agreement. Run it on a project you know. If you cannot answer **row three or seven** from a document, you have found something to fix.
notes.92: A good course turns the lens on itself. Read the five objections and their weights. The fourth, that the analysis can excuse domestic elites, has most force in South Asia. None is a reason to discard the analysis. Hold it **alongside class, caste and gender**.
notes.93: Local structures can be unequal too: caste, patriarchy, gerontocracy. Test romantic claims with the reality-check column. Row four matters most: for a Dalit household the distant state has sometimes protected against local domination. Remember that **decolonial language can be recruited by reaction**.
notes.94: Essentialism treats Western and indigenous as fixed, pure and opposed, which rebuilds the binary Orientalism made. Bhabha's hybridity reminds you that knowledge has always travelled and mixed. Watch the fourth row: **one person invited to speak for a region** burdens the individual and spares the institution.
notes.95: Two positions hold the tension: the pessimist says reform is capture, and the pragmatist says imperfect change beats paralysis. The third position, wrong question, points to trade, debt and climate. The deck leaves it open. **Work the second position while keeping the first two objections in view.**
notes.96: Co-optation adopts the language and leaves the structures. Judge by power and money moved, never by vocabulary. The fourth sign is a specific harm: unpaid staff of colour asked to lead the work. Participation and sustainability **travelled the same route** from argument to boilerplate.
notes.97: The table lists Fanon, Said, Spivak, Quijano, Escobar and Ambedkar. Ambedkar is usually absent from such lists. Reading him alongside the canon is the fastest correction to **romanticisation**, and he made the argument from inside the anti-colonial movement.
notes.98: Choose reading by the time you have. An afternoon: Spivak or Fanon's chapter on national consciousness. A week: Escobar chapters 1 to 3. For an organisational agenda, practitioner material you can circulate without a seminar is **the most immediately usable**.
notes.99: Five things to keep. Development has colonial roots. Coloniality outlived colonialism. Knowledge hierarchies are exercises of power. Follow the money and the decision rights. **Name internal hierarchies too.** The fourth converts into practice, so work through slide 90's questions in good faith.
